subject: truncated data works with mean or sd, but not both

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: truncated data works with mean or sd, but not both
parts:
I've been exploring some models for truncated data
and am more convinced than ever we need some diagnostics
for what NUTS/HMC is doing.

The simplest model estimates the mean only:

------------
data {
real U;
int<lower=1> N;
real<upper = U> y[N];
}
parameters {
real mu;
}
model {
for (n in 1:N)
y[n] ~ normal(mu,1) T[,0];
}
-------------

That T[,0] restricts the normal to (-inf,0]. There's
no prior on mu.

Around 500 data points were generated in R in the obvious way:

U <- 0
y_raw <- rnorm(1000,0,1)
y <- y_raw[y_raw < 0]
N <- length(y)

It works just fine and all the gradients check out and
the error's about what you'd expect.

If I fix mu at its true value 0 and add a sigma parameter
for sd, everything still works OK, even without a prior
on sigma:

--------------
parameters {
real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model {
for (n in 1:N)
y[n] ~ normal(0,sigma) T[,0];
}
---------------

But if I also treat sigma as a parameter, even with
a proper prior (though one that's uniform on
a small fixed range) on both sigma and mu, things
go wonky.

------------------
parameters {
real<lower=0,upper=2> sigma;
real mu;
}
model {
mu ~ normal(0,1);
for (n in 1:N)
y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma) T[,0];
}
------------------

I get some warnings about sigma=0 and mu=inf to begin,
then things settle down, then both the
estimates for sigma and mu wind up too large (around 1
for mu instead of 0 and around 1.25
for sigma instead of 1).

With sigma defined on [0,2], its unconstrained zero-init
will be 1, and with mu unconstrained, its zero-init
will be 0.

What's somewhat disturbing is the value of the gradient:

TEST GRADIENT MODE

Log probability=79.0865

param idx value model finite diff error
0 0 -3.00002 -3.00002 -4.88227e-07
1 0 16.9871 16.9871 -4.42688e-08

What I'm wondering is why there's a positive gradient for sigma (the
second parameter)? Things seem to be going the right way in
general:

TEST GRADIENT MODE

Log probability=-462.455

param idx value model finite diff error
0 -1.82834 826.009 826.009 4.62399e-06
1 -0.409461 414.698 414.698 -3.6559e-06

This init has mu way too low, so there's a big positive gradient. But
there's also a big positive gradient on sigma. I assume that's to
account for the bad prediction of mu at that point?

I'm having similar issues with censored models, for what
it's worth.

I just added unit tests for normal_p, and everything checks out
vs. R., so I don't think the problem is there. And the finite
diffs all check out, so it seems unlikely to be the gradients, either.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] truncated data works with mean or sd, but not both
parts:
I also realized why I was seeing so many rejections.
The simple models I've been looking at have had
median tree depth of one, so rejection rate is roughly
equal to average rejection rate on the second half of
the trees.

Now onto the real issue.

On 9/5/12 1:24 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
> Odd, I got perfectly reasonable results when I ran this modelï¿½samples

> for mu in the range of about (-0.5, 1.5) and samples for sigma in the
> range of about (0.8, 1.5).

I like that answer better than mine :-)

Maybe I messed up the data simulation, but it looks
OK to me plotted in R. I checked the model and data
in at:

src/models/basic_estimators/truncated_normal.stan
/truncated_normal.Rdata

Would you (Matt) mind running the checked in version to see
if it gives you OK results?

Here's what I get after 50K samples in a single
chain (though running longer or more chains
doesn't matter -- it settles on this answer
pretty quickly). Here's what the output looks
like, with simulated mu = 0, sigma = 1:

> quantile(tns$mu)
0% 25% 50% 75% 100%
-0.1016810 0.5404598 0.8620630 1.2935150 3.7038100

> quantile(tns$sigma)
0% 25% 50% 75% 100%
0.961492 1.225290 1.332955 1.457465 1.974080

> colMeans(tns)
lp__ treedepth__ stepsize__ mu sigma
80.4058466 1.3740000 0.1573470 0.9808178 1.3553201

I have switched to the latest compilers on Mountain
Lion. I never used to question the compiler or system
before I moved to C++!

- Bob
